definition: Truly what it claims to be, rather than a copy, fake, or imitation.
example: Experts confirmed that the faded map was authentic, drawn by a ship's navigator in 1790.
nuance: Authentic stresses a proven origin or faithfulness to a tradition, while genuine more broadly means real or sincere.
prompt: An appraiser examines a portrait said to be more than two hundred years old.
options: Tests of the canvas showed the portrait was authentic, not a later copy.
The appraiser called the portrait authentic once she proved a forger had painted it last spring.
The portrait was authentic because it was the largest painting in the whole auction.
The appraiser was authentic enough to sign contracts on the museum's behalf.
reasons: Scientific evidence that the work is no reproduction confirms it is the real thing.
A recent forgery is the opposite of a work that truly is what it claims to be.
Size says nothing about whether a painting is real or fake.
Having permission to act for others is being authorized, not authentic.

practice.prompt: A traveler wants to taste a regional dish the way local families cook it.
options: The chef called his stew authentic, though he had invented it that morning from canned soups.
The stew was authentic because the waiter brought it out faster than any other dish.
The café felt authentic thanks to its plastic palm trees and staff in rented costumes.
The village cook made an authentic stew with her grandmother's recipe and local herbs.
reasons: A new mix of canned products is an imitation, not the traditional dish.
Quick service has no bearing on whether food follows a real tradition.
Staged props and costumes create a fake atmosphere, not a real one.
A traditional family recipe and local ingredients keep the dish true to its roots.
